keyVerseText: And it shall come to pass, that the fishers shall stand upon it from Engedi even unto Eneglaim; they shall be a place to spread forth nets; their fish shall be according to their kinds, as the fish of the great sea, exceeding many.
rootMeaning: The term עֵין עֶגְלַיִם (ʻÊyn ʻEglayim) is composed of two Hebrew elements: עַיִן (ʻayin), meaning 'fountain' or 'spring,' and the dual form of עֵגֶל (ʻêgel), meaning 'calf' or 'bullock.' Literally, this phrase translates as 'fountain of the two calves,' suggesting a place associated with a natural water source and perhaps symbolic imagery of calves. This literal sense enriches the understanding beyond a mere place name by evoking vitality and nourishment linked to the imagery of calves, which are young, lively animals near maturity.
usageInScripture: The term עֵין עֶגְלַיִם appears only once in Scripture, specifically in Ezekiel 47:10, where it is rendered as 'Eneglaim' or 'even unto Eneglaim.' Its singular occurrence as a geographic location near the Dead Sea indicates a specific, though uncertain, site known to the original audience. The consistent translation as a proper place name emphasizes its role as a boundary marker in a prophetic vision rather than a common noun.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding עֵין עֶגְלַיִם as 'fountain of the two calves' highlights the biblical motif of life-giving water and provision in a region often associated with barrenness. This name, marking a place on the Dead Sea, points to God's promise of restoration and abundance even in desolate places. The imagery of calves, young and vigorous animals, may also reflect God's nurturing care and the vitality He brings to His people. For the Christian faith, this underscores God's sovereign ability to bring life and fruitfulness through His Spirit, fulfilling His covenant promises.
keyVerseReflection: Ezekiel 47:10 describes fishers standing from Engedi to Eneglaim, spreading nets and catching abundant fish as in the great sea. The mention of Eneglaim, 'fountain of the two calves,' marks the extent of the life-giving waters flowing from the temple vision. This place name contributes to the sense of divine provision and flourishing, illustrating how God's restoration transforms even the Dead Sea region into a place teeming with life and blessing.
